title: Meal Prepping on a Tight Budget
summary: Two hours on Sunday saves you nine $18 lunches and the daily decision-fatigue of figuring out what to eat broke.

sections.title: The Moment
sections.value: It's Wednesday, 12:40pm, and you're standing in the food court between the library and your next tute. The sushi place is $14 for two rolls. The dumpling place is $16. The salad place is $18 and the lettuce somehow looks tired. You do the maths in your head: this is the fourth lunch like this in five days, and the maths gets worse every time you do it.

sections.title: The Feeling
sections.value:
There's a particular kind of broke that comes from a thousand small decisions that each felt fine in the moment. The $14 here, the $9 coffee there. None of them are extravagant. Together they're the reason your account balance ends every fortnight in a place that surprises you.

Meal prep gets pitched as either an Instagram aesthetic (twelve identical glass containers, perfectly arranged) or a martyr's punishment (cold rice and steamed broccoli all week). It's neither. It's a way of making one decision once instead of fourteen decisions tired.

sections.title: What nobody told you
sections.value:
**You don't have to prep meals. You have to prep one base.**

The trap of "meal prep" is the word *meal* — the assumption you have to plan twelve complete dinners. You don't. The version that actually works for broke twenty-somethings is: cook one large pot of one thing on Sunday. Eat it across the week with rotating cheap add-ons.

One pot of mince and tomato sauce becomes spaghetti, becomes nachos, becomes a jacket potato, becomes a wrap. One pot of curry becomes rice-and-curry, becomes curry-and-roti, becomes curry-baked-potato. One tray of roasted veg goes into anything.

The word for this isn't meal prep. It's *base prep*. And it's the difference between something you'll keep doing in week three and something you'll abandon by Wednesday.

sections.title: How it actually works
sections.value:
**1. Pick one base, not seven meals.** A pot of bolognese. A pot of dahl. A pot of chicken-and-rice. A tray of roasted veg. Anything that gives you 5–6 servings out of one cook.

**2. Shop for the base, not for the week.** A typical bolognese base is mince, onion, garlic, tinned tomatoes, dried herbs — under $15 at ALDI for the whole pot. Dahl is even cheaper: a kilo of red lentils, an onion, a tin of tomatoes, a few spices.

**3. Cook it once. On a Sunday afternoon. While doing something else.** The pot doesn't need you. Put it on, put on a podcast, fold laundry. Forty minutes later you have the week.

**4. Portion it cold.** Five containers, fridge. The two you won't eat by Thursday go in the freezer — labeled, because by Friday you'll have forgotten what's in there.

**5. Buy *cheap rotating add-ons* for the variety.** A bag of rice ($3). A loaf of bread ($3). A bag of frozen veg ($4). A block of cheese ($6). A bag of tortillas ($4). The base is the same; the add-on is what changes.

### The bit nobody mentions

The goal isn't *cooking*. It's removing decisions. By Tuesday lunchtime, the value of your Sunday cook isn't the $80 you saved — it's that you didn't have to *think* about lunch. Decision fatigue is what makes broke people spend money. Take the decision off the table once and a lot of the spending stops on its own.

If the prep itself feels like a chore, halve the ambition. One pot. One Sunday. Five lunches. That's it. Scale only when it stops feeling like work.
